ORDER
PER HON’BLE MRS. SEEMA GUPTA, TECHNICAL MEMBER
IA NO. 890 OF 2024
(interim relief)
1. The present Interlocutory Application has been filed by M/s. Hyderabad
MSW Energy Solutions Private Limited (“Appellant”) seeking interim relief in
Appeal No. 85 of 2024, filed against the Order dated 02.01.2024 passed by the
Telangana State Electricity Regulatory Commission (“State
Commission/TSERC”) in O.P. No. 73 of 2022. The dispute in the Appeal, inter
alia, relates to the applicability of the threshold Plant Load Factor (“PLF”) to the
energy generated and delivered from the Appellant’s 19.8 MW RDF-based Waste-
to-Energy Plant at Jawaharnagar, Hyderabad, under the Power Purchase
Agreement (“PPA”) dated 19.02.2020 executed with Southern Power Distribution
Page 2 of 17

Oder in IA No.890 of 2024 in Appeal No.85 of 2024
Company of Telangana Limited (“TSSPDCL/Respondent No. 2”). The generic
tariff, applicable to the Appellant’s power project, was determined by the State
Commission vide its Tariff Order dated 18.04.2020. The Generation Plant
achieved Commercial Operation Date (“COD”) on 20.08.2020.
2. The Appellant had approached the State Commission in O.P. No. 73 of 2022
raising, inter alia, the issue of payment for energy delivered beyond the Normative
PLF mentioned in the Generic Tariff Order. The State Commission, vide its Order
dated 02.01.2024, rejected the reliefs sought by the Appellant, pursuant to which
the Appellant preferred the present Appeal.
3. Appellant has also filed present application seeking following interim reliefs:-
a) Direct Respondent No. 2 to make payment for energy delivered up to the
contracted capacity in terms of the PPA dated 19.02.2020;
b) Direct Respondent No. 2 to release the outstanding amounts claimed by
the Appellant in the present application;
c) Direct Respondent No. 2 to refrain from imposing the disputed threshold
PLF restriction on the energy bills raised by the Appellant till the disposal
of the accompanying Appeal;
d) Restrain Respondent No. 2 from taking any coercive action, including
restraining the generation of power from the Appellant's 19.8 MW RDF-
based Waste-to-Energy Plant and/or preventing the Appellant from
selling electricity to third parties, till the disposal of the accompanying
Appeal; and
Page 3 of 17

Oder in IA No.890 of 2024 in Appeal No.85 of 2024
e) Pass such further or other order(s) as this Hon’ble Tribunal may deem fit
and proper in the facts and circumstances of the present case and in the
interest of justice.
SUBMISSIONS URGED ON BEHALF OF PARTIES
4. Learned Senior Counsel for the Appellant submits that the limited issue is
whether the normative Plant Load Factor (“PLF”) of 65%, 75% and 80%, adopted
by the State Commission in the Generic Tariff Order dated 18.04.2020 for the
purpose of determination of the levelised tariff of Rs. 7.84/kWh, can be treated as
a ceiling on the quantum of Delivered Energy for which Respondent No. 2 is liable
to make payment. According to the Appellant, neither the PPA nor the Tariff Order
provides for any such restriction. PPA dated 19.02.2020 expressly governs both,
the quantum of energy to be purchased and the manner of payment. Explanation
2 to Article 1.10 provides that the Delivered Energy in a billing month shall be
limited to the energy calculated at 100% PLF of the net exportable capacity, after
accounting for auxiliary consumption, contracted capacity and operating hours.
Article 2.1 obligates Respondent No. 2 to purchase all the Delivered Energy at the
Interconnection Point, and Article 2.2 provides for payment at the tariff determined
by the State Commission for the net energy delivered. Further, the exclusion
contemplated under Article 2.2, according to the Appellant, relates only to energy
delivered beyond the contracted capacity and not to energy supplied beyond the
normative PLF.
5. It is submitted that Schedule-1 to the PPA records the Project capacity as
19.8 MW, of which 2.178 MW is towards auxiliary consumption and the balance
17.622 MW is available for export to the grid for sale to the DISCOM at the
Page 4 of 17

Oder in IA No.890 of 2024 in Appeal No.85 of 2024
Interconnection Point. It is, therefore, contended that the exportable capacity
stipulated under the PPA is distinct from the normative PLF adopted for the
purpose of tariff determination. The interpretation sought to be placed by
Respondent No. 2 would render the express reference to 100% PLF in
Explanation 2 to Article 1.10 otiose. It is submitted that if payment for energy was
intended to cease upon the Appellant achieving the normative PLF of 65%, 75%
or 80%, there was no occasion for the PPA to expressly provide for Delivered
Energy up to 100% PLF. The Appellant submits that the harmonious construction
of the PPA and the Tariff Order is that the PPA determines the quantum of billable
Delivered Energy, whereas the Tariff Order determines the applicable tariff.
6. It is submitted by Learned Senior Counsel for the Appellant, State
Commission determined generic tariff for Waste-to energy plant under Section 62
based on normative technical and financial parameters. Under Issue No. 4,
stakeholders sought an incentive for achieving PLF higher than the normative
level, with reference inter alia to the treatment afforded to biomass projects. The
State Commission approved normative PLFs of 65%/75%/80% in Para 34 and
declined the proposal for any incentive beyond the normative PLF in Para 35.
Significantly, however, Para 35 neither states that the tariff would cease once the
normative PLF was achieved, nor that electricity generated thereafter would be
supplied without consideration, nor that the contractual ceiling of 100% PLF stood
substituted by the normative PLFs of 65%/75%/80%. Further, in the operative
portion of the Tariff Order, while determining a levelised tariff of Rs. 7.84/kWh for
RDF-based projects, the Commission did not prescribe any annual block or
quantum of units to which the tariff alone would apply. Thus, the tariff
determination contains no quantity cap, and the normative PLF operates only as
a normative parameter for tariff determination and not as a ceiling on the quantum
Page 5 of 17

Oder in IA No.890 of 2024 in Appeal No.85 of 2024
of electricity for which the determined tariff is payable. The rejection of the
proposal for an additional “incentive” for generation beyond the normative PLF
cannot, in the absence of express words, be construed as overriding the pre-
existing contractual arrangement approved by the State Commission. Prior to
issuance of the Generic Tariff Order dated 18.04.2020, the Commission had
approved the PPA containing Explanation 2 to Article 1.10, which expressly
defined Delivered Energy up to 100% PLF and the PPA was executed on
19.02.2020.
7. Learned senior counsel placed reliance on Para 3.3 of the Explanatory
Memorandum to the CERC (Terms and Conditions for Tariff Determination from
Renewable Energy Sources) Regulations, 2017, which provides that “any
generation beyond threshold PLF shall also receive same tariff”, recognising that
the risks and costs associated with project sizing, location, etc. are borne by the
developer, a principle reflected in the CERC renewable-energy tariff framework
since 2009 and consistent with the 100% mandatory procurement regime.
8. The State Commission, in exercise of its adjudicatory jurisdiction under the
Impugned Order, could not introduce into the approved PPA a commercial
restriction which neither the parties incorporated nor the Commission expressly
imposed through the Tariff Order. Further, the reasoning drawn therefrom, that the
contractual expression “100% PLF” could not be given its express meaning is also
untenable. Learned counsel placed Reliance on “Haryana Power Purchase
Centre v. Sasan Power Ltd” (2024) 1 SCC 247, ; “GMR Warora Energy Ltd.
v. CERC” (2023) 10 SCC 401, and “Nabha Power Ltd. v. PSPCL’ (2018) 11
SCC 508.
Page 6 of 17

Oder in IA No.890 of 2024 in Appeal No.85 of 2024
9. Further, the reliance placed in the Impugned Order upon O.P.(SR) No.116
of 2022 is equally unsustainable, since the present proceedings had already been
reserved for orders on 04.04.2023, whereas the said order was rendered
subsequently on 30.10.2023 and was thereafter set aside by this Hon’ble Tribunal
in Appeal No.63 of 2024 and remanded for fresh consideration; significantly, upon
remand, the State Commission, by order dated 04.08.2025 in O.P. No.21 of 2024,
specifically held, on the basis of actual generation data, that the existing plant had
generated 24 MW without augmentation.
10. It is submitted that the clause 6.4 of the National Tariff Policy, 2016 expressly
mandates compulsory procurement of 100% of the power produced from all
Waste-to-Energy plants at the tariff determined by the Appropriate Commission,
which mandate was given regulatory effect by the State Commission through
Regulation 3.8 of the RPPO Regulations, 2018 and subsequently Regulation 3(7)
of the RPPO Regulations, 2022, requiring Distribution Licensees in Telangana to
compulsorily procure 100% power produced from WtE plants. The special and
mandatory character of the WtE regime stands further recognized by the Hon’ble
Supreme Court in “Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Gagan Narang & Ors.,”
2025 INSC 2, particularly paras which recognizes the interplay between Section
86(1)(e) of the Electricity Act and the Solid Waste Management Rules, as well as
the mandatory 100% procurement regime and the larger public interest served by
WtE projects in reducing the burden on landfills and facilitating waste disposal.
The statutory, regulatory and policy framework therefore reinforces the contractual
interpretation and renders untenable any construction whereby electricity
mandatorily procured and accepted by the Distribution Licensee becomes
“gratuitous” merely upon crossing the normative PLF. Accordingly, the finding in
the Impugned Order treating normative PLF as a ceiling on payment is liable to
Page 7 of 17

Oder in IA No.890 of 2024 in Appeal No.85 of 2024
be set aside, and Respondent No. 2 ought to be directed to pay the applicable
tariff for all Delivered Energy generated beyond the normative PLF and up to
100% PLF of net exportable capacity, in accordance with Explanation 2 to Article
1.10.
11. Per contra, Learned Counsel appearing for Respondent No. 2 submitted
that, under Clause 3 of the PPA, the power is to be purchased at the tariff
determined by the TGERC, while Articles 2.1 and 2.2 further stipulate that the
“Delivered Energy” shall be purchased at the tariff determined by the TGERC from
time to time, and the orders of the TGERC are enforceable in their entirety. Article
1.22 of the PPA defines Plant Load Factor (PLF) and specifically provides that the
PLF shall be determined by the TGERC . Pursuant thereto, the TGERC, in its Tariff
Order dated 18.04.2020, considered the issue of PLF under Issue No. 4 and, after
considering the stakeholders’ submissions, approved normative PLFs of 65% for
the first year, 75% for the second year and 80% from the third year onwards, while
expressly declining the proposal for any incentive for generation beyond the
approved PLF. The said determination has attained finality, no party having
challenged Issue No. 4, and is consequently binding on the parties. Accordingly,
any reference to PLF under the PPA must be understood with reference to the
PLF determined by the TGERC, and no deviation therefrom can be permitted.
12. Learned Counsel for Respondent No. 2 places reliance upon the judgment
of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in State of U.P. v. Ram Sukhi Devi, (2005) 9 SCC
733, to contend that final relief ought not to be granted at the interlocutory stage.
It is submitted that where the grant of interim relief would substantially result in
allowing the main Appeal itself, such relief ought not to be granted.
Page 8 of 17

Oder in IA No.890 of 2024 in Appeal No.85 of 2024
13. It is submitted that the Appellant has selectively relied upon Clause 6.4(2)
of the National Tariff Policy, 2016, which requires the Distribution Licensee to
procure 100% of the power from WtE plants at the tariff determined by the
Appropriate Commission. Respondent No. 2 is strictly complying with the Tariff
Order dated 18.04.2020 passed by the TGERC and, consequently, with Clause
6.4(2) of the National Tariff Policy as well as the applicable RPPO obligations
within the tariff framework determined by the Commission. Appellant has failed to
establish any prima facie case, balance of convenience or irreparable loss or
injury warranting interim relief, particularly when Respondent No. 2 is acting
strictly in accordance with the binding Tariff Order prescribing the applicable PLF
ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION
14. We have heard Mr Sanjay Sen, Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
Appellant and Mr Rajat Shrivastav, learned counsel for Respondent No 1 and Mr
Abhinav Rav, Learned counsel on behalf Respondent No 2 and perused material
on record, written submissions filed by parties. The detailed rival submissions
and the entitlement of the Appellant to the amounts claimed by it, including the
issue relating to applicability of the threshold PLF under the PPA, shall be
considered while adjudicating the Appeal on merits. At this stage, the question
before us is limited to whether an interim arrangement is warranted during the
pendency of the Appeal if yes then what interim arrangement.
15. We also take note that Appellant in its Application for stay in paragraph 3
and 4 have stated that
Page 9 of 17

Oder in IA No.890 of 2024 in Appeal No.85 of 2024
3. It is pertinent to mention that vide Order dated 21.05.2024, this Hon’ble Tribunal has
after extensively hearing the Applicant on the limited issue of applicability of threshold
Plant Load Factor (PLF) on the delivered energy under the terms of the PPA dated
19.02.2020, observed that, a prima facie case seems to exist for an interim
arrangement to be put in place; however, since the Applicant has not sought expressly
any consequential relief in terms of the amount claimed as due, in the event the
relief(s) as sought under IA No. 312 of 2024 are allowed, it would be difficult to
translate the same in terms of recovery of the amount sought to be claimed by the
Applicant.
4. That in view of the above, present Application is being filed seeking relief in terms of
a plausible interim arrangement in view of the last hearing dated 21.05.2024. The
same is also brought on record vide the present application.
16. It is a matter of concern that the Appellant has sought to rely upon the order
dated 21.05.2024 as if it contained an observation regarding existence of a prima
facie case for interim arrangement. A plain reading of the said order reveals that
it dealt solely with condonation of delay in filing the rejoinder in IA No. 312 of
2014, subject to payment of cost, and no such observation was made. The
Appellant’s assertion is therefore factually incorrect. Parties before this Tribunal
are expected to exercise due care and accuracy in their pleadings. Any attempt
to misstate or misrepresent the record not only misleads the adjudicatory process
but also undermines the integrity of proceedings. The Appellant is accordingly
reprimanded and cautioned to scrupulously verify the record before making
submissions in future, failing which appropriate consequences may ensue.
17. We shall now proceed to deliberate the issue in the present application. The
grant or refusal of interlocutory relief is covered by three well established
principles viz., (1) whether the Appellant has made out a prima facie case, (2)
whether the balance of convenience is in their favour i.e., whether it would cause
greater inconvenience to them if interim relief is not granted than the
Page 10 of 17

Oder in IA No.890 of 2024 in Appeal No.85 of 2024
inconvenience which the opposite party would be put to if it is granted, and (3)
whether the Appellant would suffer irreparable injury. With the first condition as a
sine qua non, atleast two conditions should be satisfied by the Appellant
conjunctively, and a mere proof of fulfilment of one of the three conditions does
not entitle them to the grant of interlocutory relief in their favour. (Nawab Mir
Barkat Ali Khan v. Nawab Zulfiquar Jah Bahadur, AIR 1975 AP 187; Gone
Rajamma v. Chennamaneni Mohan Rao, (2010) 3 ALD 175; Kishoresinh
Ratansinh Jadeja v. Maruti Corpn, (2009) 11 SCC 229; Best Sellers Retail (India)
Private Ltd. v. Aditya Birla Nuvo Ltd., (2012) 6 SCC 792; State of Mizoram v. Pooja
Fortune Private Limited, 2019 SCC OnLine SC 1741).
18. The main issue in this application and the Appeal pertains to the issue
whether Appellant is entitled to tariff for the energy generated beyond
65%/75%/80% PLF as mentioned in the Generic Tariff Order. In this context, it is
apposite to extract relevant paragraphs of the PPA.
1.10 "Delivered Energy" means with respect to any billing month, the Kilo
Watt hours (KWh) of electrical energy generated by the project and delivered
to the DISCOM at the interconnection point, as defined in clause 1.18 and as
measured by the energy meters at the interconnection point during that billing
month at the designated substation of TSTRANSCO or the DISCOM:
Explanation 1: For removal of doubts, the delivered energy, excludes all
energy consumed in the project, by the main plant and equipment, lightning
and other loads of the project from the energy generated and as recorded by
the energy meter at interconnection point.
Explanation 2: The delivered energy in a billing month shall be limited to the
energy calculated at 100% PLF of net exportable capacity that is after
deducting capacities for auxiliary consumption from the installed capacity as
mentioned in this agreement for sale to DISCOM, based on the contracted
capacity in KW multiplied with number of hours and fraction thereof, the
project is in operation during that billing month. Whenever generation
exceeds by installed capacity such energy delivered into the grid by the
Page 11 of 17

Oder in IA No.890 of 2024 in Appeal No.85 of 2024
project above 100% PLF during such period shall be considered payment or
otherwise in terms of the rules and regulations in vogue.
Explanation 3: The delivered energy shall be purchased by the DISCOM at
a tariff for that year stipulated in Article 2.2 of this agreement.
1.22 "Plant Load Factor (PLF)" means the ratio of total KWh (units) of power
generated by plant in a tariff year, as decided by TSERC and contracted
capacity in KW multiplied with number of hours in the same tariff year;
ARTICLE 2
PURCHASE OF DELIVERED ENERGY AND TARIFF
2.1 All the delivered energy at the interconnection point for sale to DISCOM
(net capacity) will be purchased at the tariff provided for in Article 2.2 from
and after the date of commercial operation of the project. Title to delivered
energy purchased shall pass from the company to the DISCOM at the
interconnection point.
2.2 The company shall be paid the tariff for the net energy delivered at the
interconnection point for sale to DISCOM at the tariff as determined by
TSERC from time to time. No tariff will be paid for the energy delivered at the
interconnection point beyond contracted capacity. The orders of TSERC are
enforceable in entirety and shall be considered for the purposes of
computation of tariff
19. From the bare reading of these provisions, it appears that delivered energy
pertains to the energy delivered at the interconnection point and shall be
purchased by the Discom at a tariff determined by TSERC and no tariff beyond
the contracted capacity, which is stated to be 19.8 MW in terms of referred PPA
dated 19.02.2020, shall be payable by the Discom. The PPA further defines the
Plant load Factor (PLF), which shall be total kWh of power generated by plant in
a tariff year as decided by the TSERC.
Page 12 of 17

Oder in IA No.890 of 2024 in Appeal No.85 of 2024
20. We take note that State Commission, vide its order dated 18.04.2020, has
determined Generic tariff for the electricity generated from Refuse Derived Fuel
(RDF) based power projects, such as that of Appellant’s project. The tariff Order
takes cognizance of the Tariff Policy 2016, which mandates Distribution licensee
to compulsorily procure 100 % power produced from all Waste – to Energy (WtE)
plant in the State in the ratio of their procurement of power from all sources. The
State Commission in the tariff order has determined levelized tariff of Rs 7.84 per
kwh applicable for RDF based projects achieving COD during the period from FY
2021-FY 2023-24 for a period of 20 years from COD. There is no dispute that tariff
determined in this generic tariff order is applicable for Appellant’s Project. Further
the generic tariff order approves PLF of 65 % for first Year, 75 % for second year
and 80 % for third year and onwards. We also take note that stakeholders request
of incentive for achieving PLF higher than norms in line with approved incentive
of 25 paise/kWh for bio mass and MSW plants, was not approved by State
Commission and it stated that “ The commission does not subscribe to the stake
holders submission that providing incentive for higher PLF than the approved
PLF”.
21. Learned counsel for the Respondent has contended that PLF should be
considered in terms of PLF determined by the State Commission and the State
Commission has also not subscribed to the stakeholders submissions to provide
incentive for higher PLF than approved and accordingly prayer in the present IA
seeking payment for energy delivered beyond the approved PLF is not
maintainable.
22. It is pertinent to note that Waste-to-Energy plants, such as that of
Appellant’s plant serve a dual public purpose. They contribute to sustainable
Page 13 of 17

Oder in IA No.890 of 2024 in Appeal No.85 of 2024
waste management by reducing the quantum of municipal solid waste otherwise
destined for landfills, thereby mitigating attendant environmental hazards.
Simultaneously, they generate electricity from such waste, augmenting the
energy mix with a renewable source and reducing dependence on conventional
fossil fuels. The technology thus advances the twin objectives of environmental
protection and energy security, while also promoting circular economy principles.
These advantages underscore the larger public interest embedded in
Waste-to-Energy projects (WtE). Importance of WtE project has been
acknowledged in Tariff policy 2016, and Generic tariff Order dated 18.04.2020
also refers to the Tariff Policy. Further State Commission in the generic Tariff
order, while determining two part tariff has stated that tariff structure adopted by
the commission is fairly conducive for promotion of RDF based power projects.
23. From the perusal of Generic order, prima facie we feel there is no specific
exclusion/bar/ restriction for purchase of electricity beyond the Normative PLF.
Respondents have contended that denial of incentive of 25 Paise/kWh for
achieving PLF more than Normative is indicative that purchase of energy from
WtE project is to be limited to normative PLF. However, our attention has not been
brought to any deliberation/observation in the generic tariff order, that State
Commission while rejecting the said incentive, has made categorical statement
that energy generation and consequently its payment is capped at Normative
PLF.
24. In general, the incentive mechanism of say X Paise per kWh, as provided
in a tariff order, is intended to reward generating stations that achieve Plant Load
Factor (PLF) above the normative benchmark fixed therein. The normative PLF
represents the standard level of performance expected of such plants. Where the
Page 14 of 17

Oder in IA No.890 of 2024 in Appeal No.85 of 2024
actual PLF achieved exceeds this normative level, the excess generation is
entitled to incentive at the prescribed rate. This arrangement ensures that
generators are encouraged to optimize their operations, thereby contributing
additional energy to the grid, while simultaneously aligning regulatory objectives
with consumer interest in enhanced availability of power. The incentive thus
operates as a performance-linked measure, reinforcing efficiency and reliability
in the sector. In the case of WtE projects, it shall also mean better waste
management.
25. Further, on a specific query addressed to the Respondent Discom
regarding the meaning and scope of the approved incentive of Rs 0.25 per kWh,
which appears to have been applied to other categories of generation projects
under certain tariff orders, no explanation was forthcoming either during the
hearing of the Application or in the written submissions filed. In the absence of
any clarification, at this stage, we are unable to accept the contention advanced
by the Respondents that rejection of incentive substantiate that tariff beyond the
Normative PLF is not applicable. This aspect, however, shall require detailed
deliberation at the time of final adjudication of the Appeal.
26. It is further noted that denial of purchase of energy beyond the Normative
PLF, at this stage, would effectively constrain the Appellant’s plant, though
capable of burning additional waste and generating energy beyond the Normative
PLF, to operate only up to the Normative PLF, since no charges for such excess
energy are payable under the Impugned Order. Such denial may result in
underutilization of the plant’s capacity despite its technical capability to burn more
waste and generate additional energy, without conclusively deciding the issue,
which shall be done at the final hearing of the Appeal
Page 15 of 17

Oder in IA No.890 of 2024 in Appeal No.85 of 2024
27. Further, it is also not in dispute that energy more than the normative PLF
has been generated by the Appellant and consumed by the Respondent and
Appellant in present application is restricting its claim on the energy generated
up to the Contracted capacity as specified in the PPA dated 19.02.2020.
28. In view of the foregoing deliberations, it is evident that the substantive
issues arising out of the provisions of the Power Purchase Agreement, the
Generic Tariff Order, and the Tariff Policy, 2016, require detailed examination and
adjudication at the stage of final hearing, with due regard to the judicial
pronouncements cited by the parties. At this stage, however, we are satisfied that
the Appellant has made out a prima facie case warranting interim protection, and
the balance of convenience lies in its favour. We are, however, not inclined to
grant the full levelised tariff as per the Generic Tariff Order dated 18.04.2020 for
energy generated beyond the Normative PLF and up to the contracted capacity,
as sought in the present application, since such determination must await final
adjudication of the Appeal. We, however, take note that Generic Tariff Order
dated 18.04.2020 is a two part tariff, in which State Commission had determined
the Levelised tariff of Rs 7.84 /kwh comprising of levelised fixed cost of Rs
3.42/kwh and levelised variable cost of Rs 4.42/kwh. Accordingly, in the interest
of justice and to prevent irreparable prejudice pending disposal of the Appeal,
Appellant shall be paid the levelised variable tariff in terms of Generic Tariff Order
dated 18.04.2020.
29. In view of above deliberations, in the interim, we direct that the Respondent
– Discom shall pay the levelised variable cost as per the Generic Tariff Order
dated 18.04.2020 for the energy generated beyond the Normative PLF and up to
Page 16 of 17

Oder in IA No.890 of 2024 in Appeal No.85 of 2024
the contracted capacity to the Appellant. Respondent – Discom is further directed
to make payment on this basis for the past period within six weeks from the
receipt of this order, and for the future, the same is payable in the respective
invoices.
30. Needless to state that payment made by Respondent No 2 i.e. Discom to
the Appellant with this interim arrangement, shall be subject to the outcome of the
main appeal.
31. With the above observations, the IA No. 890 of 2024 is disposed of.
APPEAL No. 85 OF 2024
Registry to verify if the pleadings in the appeal are complete and then
include it in the ‘List of Finals’, to be taken up from there, in its turn.
